hints: Think about bonding in each allotrope, and ask yourself which one has no spare p-orbital electrons to delocalise.
Remember that in diamond each carbon forms four single sigma bonds in a tetrahedral arrangement, using up all four outer electrons.
Contrast that with the other three structures where each carbon forms only three sigma bonds, leaving one electron free to move in a pi system.
walkthrough:
**Recall what localised means**

Think of localised as fixed in place between two atoms. Delocalised means free to move over several atoms and carry charge.

Rule to use: localised = all electrons in sigma bonds, delocalised = spare electrons in pi system

**Look at diamond bonding**

In diamond each $C$ atom is $sp^3$ hybridised and bonded to four other $C$ atoms. All four valence electrons are used in four strong sigma bonds.

$$C \text{ uses } 4 \text{ electrons in } 4 \times C-C \text{ sigma bonds}$$

**Check the other allotropes**

In graphite, graphene and buckminsterfullerene each $C$ is $sp^2$ hybridised with only three sigma bonds. The fourth electron sits in a p-orbital and is delocalised, which is why graphite and graphene conduct electricity.

options.A: Buckminsterfullerene, $C_{60}$, has each carbon bonded to three others with one delocalised electron in a pi system over the cage. It is not fully localised, so this is incorrect.
options.B: In diamond every carbon forms four tetrahedral sigma bonds with no spare electrons left over. All electrons are localised in single bonds, which is why diamond is hard and does not conduct electricity.
options.C: In graphite each carbon forms three sigma bonds within a layer, with the fourth electron delocalised between layers. This mobile electron allows conduction, so electrons are not all localised.
options.D: Graphene is a single layer of graphite with $sp^2$ bonding. Each carbon has one delocalised p-electron that moves freely across the sheet, giving excellent conductivity.
